title: Exact identified set for aggregation weights from a single observed portfolio cross-section
scope: Unrestricted CARA-normal one-security model; full characterization of response weights conditional on observed means, price and holdings.
significance: Characterizes the complete identified set, separating zero-spread investors from observed nonzero-spread traders and proving when weights are point identified.
body:
# Exact identified set for aggregation weights from one cross-section

The unrestricted-market proposition in “Even observed portfolios need not identify response weights” is correct. Its three-investor example extends to an exact characterization for any finite population. This identifies precisely which observations recover the response weights and which observations leave an open family of counterfactual responses.

Keep the source's unrestricted CARA-normal economy, with positive risk tolerances \(\tau_i=(\gamma_i\sigma_i^2)^{-1}\), fixed supply \(Q\), and observed means \(\mu_i\), clearing price \(p\), and final holdings \(q_i\). Assume \(\sum_iq_i=Q\). Define
\[
I=\{i:\mu_i\ne p\},\qquad J=\{i:\mu_i=p\}.
\]
Compatibility with this economy requires \(q_j=0\) for every \(j\in J\), and
\[
r_i:=q_i/(\mu_i-p)>0\quad(i\in I).
\]
These conditions are also sufficient. In fact, all compatible primitive vectors, with no omitted restrictions, are
\[
\tau_i=r_i\ (i\in I),\qquad \tau_j=t_j>0\ (j\in J).
\tag{A}
\]

To prove necessity, use the demand equation \(q_i=\tau_i(\mu_i-p)\). For sufficiency, choose variances equal to one and risk aversions \(1/\tau_i\). The demand equation then reproduces each holding at the observed price. Since the observed holdings sum to supply, the market clears. The strictly decreasing aggregate demand gives its unique price. Thus (A) describes actual economies, rather than merely formal candidate coefficients.

Write \(S=\sum_{i\in I}r_i\) and \(T=\sum_{j\in J}t_j\). Holding the primitive tolerances and supply fixed during a mean perturbation, the response weights are
\[
w_i=\frac{r_i}{S+T}\quad(i\in I),\qquad
w_j=\frac{t_j}{S+T}\quad(j\in J).
\tag{B}
\]
These formulas completely describe the identified set.

If \(J\) is empty, all tolerances and therefore all weights are point identified. If both \(I\) and \(J\) are nonempty, the relative weights of the observed nonzero-spread traders remain identified:
\[
w_i/w_\ell=r_i/r_\ell\quad(i,\ell\in I).
\]
Their total weight \(\alpha=\sum_{i\in I}w_i=S/(S+T)\), however, ranges over exactly \((0,1)\). Conversely, every choice of \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) and strictly positive weights on \(J\) summing to \(1-\alpha\), together with \(w_i=\alpha r_i/S\), is attained: set \(t_j=Sw_j/\alpha\). In particular the individual range for a trader \(i\in I\) is exactly \((0,r_i/S)\). None of these open endpoints is attained with finite strictly positive tolerances.

There is one important boundary case. If \(I\) is empty, compatibility forces every holding to zero and hence \(Q=0\). The admissible response vectors are then the entire strictly positive probability simplex. For a single investor that simplex consists of the single weight one. With at least two investors, each coordinate can approach zero or one but cannot equal either. If the data violate a compatibility condition, the identified set is empty; one should not interpret this as partial identification.

For the manuscript's example, \(I=\{1,3\}\), \(r_1=r_3=1\), and \(J=\{2\}\), recovering exactly \(w_1=1/(2+t)\). The general result additionally shows that a zero current position is not intrinsically uninformative: a zero position with a nonzero observed mean-price spread actually contradicts the unrestricted benchmark. The unidentified cases arise specifically at zero spreads.

This is an independent identification result inside the declared terminal-dividend model. It neither identifies trading volume without initial portfolios nor extends the weight formulas across position constraints or active-set changes. It makes no empirical calibration or external-literature claim. The constrained theorem, dynamic learning, survey errors and wealth-dependent preferences require separate analysis.

title: Order invariance and exact welfare loss with any finite number of sequential veto holders
scope: Extension of the source's two-incumbent finite-type sequential consent mechanism to n incumbents, arbitrary type correlation and any fixed public order.
significance: Proves order-independent equilibrium outcomes for arbitrary finite veto populations and an exact participation-loss formula, including absence of any positive welfare approximation ratio.
body:
# Order invariance with finitely many sequential veto holders

The manuscript's two-incumbent consent theorem has a useful extension: any fixed public order of finitely many veto holders produces the same equilibrium outcome. Correlation of waiting costs does not create an additional coordination loss. The obstruction remains individual participation, and its welfare cost admits the same exact decomposition.

Let there be \(n\ge2\) incumbents. Immediate clearing gives each \(L_i\ge0\). The fixed postponement continuation gives expected discounted payoffs \(R_i\), plus total payoff \(\Gamma\ge0\) to other agents. These expectations are independent of the cost vector. Costs \(c=(c_1,\ldots,c_n)\) have an arbitrary finite joint distribution; incumbent \(i\) privately observes \(c_i\), pays it only upon postponement, and has gain \(g_i=R_i-L_i\). Require \(c_i\ne g_i\) at every supported type. In a fixed public order, each incumbent is asked to consent; the first refusal implements immediate clearing, and all consents implement postponement. Retain the source's restrictions on outside matching and terminal decisions.

**Claim.** In every sequential equilibrium, for each positive-probability type profile, postponement occurs with probability one exactly when \(c_i<g_i\) for every \(i\); it occurs with probability zero otherwise. Consequently every public order has the same outcome distribution.

Here is a proof that explicitly handles correlation and indifferent consent decisions. At any reached decision history, incumbent \(i\)'s conditional expected gain from consent is
\[
(g_i-c_i)\Pr(\text{all later agents consent}\mid\text{history},c_i).
\tag{A}
\]
Refusal supplies the immediate benchmark. Therefore a negative-gain type can consent only when its conditional probability of eventual postponement is zero. Such types cannot occur with positive probability on a completed consent path. Thus, almost surely, actual postponement requires that all realized gains be positive.

For the reverse implication, use backward induction on the number of remaining decisions at reached histories. The final incumbent strictly consents whenever its gain is positive. Suppose later decisions implement postponement whenever all their realized gains are positive. At a reached history, consider a current positive-gain type whose posterior gives positive probability to all later gains being positive. By the induction hypothesis the probability in (A) is positive, so this incumbent strictly consents. If that posterior probability is zero, the event that all remaining gains are positive has conditional probability zero and creates no missing positive-probability profile. Because the type space and decision tree are finite, this reasoning excludes every positive-probability all-positive profile from a refusal outcome. Mixed actions at zero-probability-gain nodes do not change the result. Sequential equilibrium exists for this finite perfect-recall game, as in the source.

Put \(L=\sum_iL_i\), \(X=\sum_i(g_i-c_i)+\Gamma\), and \(A=\{c_i<g_i\text{ for all }i\}\). The consent mechanism and an informed planner able to enforce either option satisfy
\[
W_C=L+\mathbb E[X\mathbf1_A],\qquad
W_P=L+\mathbb E[X_+],
\]
and hence
\[
W_P-W_C=\mathbb E[X_+\mathbf1_{A^c}].
\tag{B}
\]
Indeed \(X>0\) on \(A\), so the two integrands agree there. This also proves \(W_C\ge L\) and shows that changing the consent order cannot repair the loss in (B).

There is no strictly positive uniform ratio \(W_C/W_P\), even with deterministic zero costs and strictly accepted terminal matches. For two incumbents take immediate payoffs \((\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\), with \(\varepsilon>0\), and continuation payoffs \((1,0)\), together with one entrant's payoff \(1\). The second incumbent strictly loses \(\varepsilon\) and vetoes; the first strictly gains for \(0<\varepsilon<1\). Thus \(W_C=2\varepsilon\) while \(W_P=2\), and the ratio tends to zero. Additional incumbents can have immediate payoff zero and strictly positive continuation payoffs without removing the veto.

This extension does not optimize over general matching rules. Transfers, private continuation values, endogenous arrivals and alternative matching deviations change (A). It supports the source's restricted mechanism result and strengthens its diagnosis: public order resolves the consent coordination issue, but cannot generally approximate enforceable welfare.

title: Removing regularity by ironing virtual readiness costs
scope: Irregular-type extension of the source's single-supplier, verifiable readiness screening model, retaining its welfare boundary, financing loss and bounded allocation.
significance: Constructs and proves an optimal truthful readiness contract when the displayed virtual cost is not monotone, with pooling determined by a convex minorant.
body:
# Removing regularity by ironing virtual readiness costs

The “Optimal regular readiness contract” theorem is sound under its stated monotonicity assumption. That assumption can be removed within the same one-dimensional model. The correction is an ironed virtual cost, with an explicit optimality proof; it is not a claim that the source's regular theorem contains an error.

Retain the source's positive continuous density on a compact type interval, its bounded readiness \(0\le k\le\bar k\), increasing concave \(C^1\) benefit \(B\), \(\kappa>0\), and financing parameter \(\lambda>0\). Let \(q=F(\theta)\), \(\theta(q)=F^{-1}(q)\), and
\[
v(q)=(1+\lambda)\theta(q)+\lambda q/f(\theta(q)),\qquad
C(q)=\int_0^qv(s)\,ds.
\]
These functions are continuous. Let \(\bar C\) be the greatest convex function lying below \(C\) on \([0,1]\), and let \(\bar v\) be its almost-everywhere derivative. Endpoint values of the derivative do not affect expected welfare. Standard one-dimensional convexity here can also be obtained by taking the lower convex hull of the graph: \(\bar C\) touches \(C\) at both endpoints, and on each connected component of \(\{C>\bar C\}\) it is affine.

Define
\[
k^I(q)=\arg\max_{0\le k\le\bar k}
\left\{B(k)-(1+\lambda)\kappa k^2/2-\bar v(q)k\right\}.
\tag{A}
\]
The maximizer exists and is unique because of the strictly concave quadratic term. Since \(\bar v\) is nondecreasing, the elementary two-maximizer inequality used in the source shows that \(k^I\) is nonincreasing. Choose its values at jumps monotonically. Consequently \(k^I(F(\theta))\) is implementable by the source lemma, with
\[
U(\theta)=\int_\theta^{\bar\theta}k^I(F(s))\,ds,\quad
t(\theta)=\theta k^I(F(\theta))+\kappa k^I(F(\theta))^2/2+U(\theta).
\tag{B}
\]

For completeness, the key inequality establishing optimality is as follows. For any feasible nonincreasing allocation \(k(q)\), put \(D=C-\bar C\ge0\). Both endpoints of \(D\) are zero. Integration by parts against the bounded-variation function \(k\) yields
\[
\int_0^1(v-\bar v)k\,dq
=-\int_{[0,1]}D\,dk\ge0,
\tag{C}
\]
because \(dk\) is a nonpositive measure. Thus replacing the original virtual cost by its ironed version weakly raises the objective of every implementable allocation. The source's Fubini calculation converts the original expected objective, after minimizing transfers, into
\[
\int_0^1\{B(k)-(1+\lambda)\kappa k^2/2-vk\}\,dq.
\]
Equation (C) bounds it above by the corresponding ironed objective. Equation (A) maximizes that upper bound pointwise.

This bound is attained by \(k^I\). On every open interval where \(D>0\), the convex minorant is affine, so \(\bar v\) is constant almost everywhere. Uniqueness of the maximizer in (A) makes \(k^I\) constant on that interval. Hence the measure \(-dk^I\) charges no point where \(D>0\); where it may charge, \(D=0\). The right side of (C) is therefore zero for \(k^I\). Its original welfare equals its ironed upper bound, proving global optimality among truthful, individually rational contracts.

For quadratic benefits \(B(k)=bk-dk^2/2\), \(d\ge0\), implementation is especially transparent:
\[
k^I(q)=\left[\frac{b-\bar v(q)}
 {d+(1+\lambda)\kappa}\right]_0^{\bar k}.
\]
Intervals on which the cumulative virtual cost lies strictly above its lower convex hull are pooling intervals. At a regular distribution, \(C\) is already convex, so \(\bar C=C\), and the construction reduces to the source theorem. Zero readiness and full-capacity portions are permitted, including types at allocation jumps; changes on probability-zero endpoint types do not alter expected welfare.

This is a substantial restricted extension, not a solution of the broader preparedness problem. It retains verifiable readiness, risk neutrality, commitment and the absence of a binding hard budget. It does not address unobservable innovation effort, correlated platform failures or competition. The source's separate hold-up game and outbreak-ambiguity claim are outside this extension. No external references or empirical quantities are certified here.
